text: This KER describes the causal relationship whereby increased DNA strand breaks lead to cell cycle disruption. DNA strand breaks include single-strand breaks (SSBs) and double-strand breaks (DSBs); DSBs are generally considered the most genotoxic lesions. Strand breaks are detected by sensor complexes that activate the apical kinases ATM (mainly in response to DSBs) and ATR (in response to single-stranded DNA at resected breaks and stalled replication forks). These kinases activate the effector kinases CHK2 and CHK1 and p53–p21 signaling, which inhibit the CDC25 phosphatases and cyclin-dependent kinases and thereby delay or arrest progression through G1/S, S, or G2/M (Hartwell and Weinert, 1989; O'Connell et al., 2000; Cuddihy and O'Connell, 2003; Jackson and Bartek, 2009; Ciccia and Elledge, 2010).  The relationship is conditional. Whether strand breaks cause a detectable disruption of the cell cycle depends on the number and type of breaks, whether they are repaired before the checkpoint response is sustained, the cell-cycle phase at the time of damage, and checkpoint competence. A single DSB at a defined genomic site can trigger a checkpoint response that delays cell cycle progression in human cells (van den Berg et al., 2018), whereas transient SSBs generated during normal DNA repair are usually resolved without arrest. If damage is repaired, arrest is reversible; persistent or irreparable damage can lead to prolonged arrest or permanent exit from the cell cycle (Jackson and Bartek, 2009). The relationship is not stressor-specific and can be triggered by ionizing radiation, oxidative stress, redox-active chemicals, metals, nanoparticles, or endogenous processes that generate strand breaks directly or indirectly.
